h: Myth in place of science: India retreats from reason
dek: In Scroll, Harsh Mander writes that the scientific temper is India's centuries-old heritage, and that it is being crushed today through textbooks, platforms of power and the killing of rationalists.
ank: Duty of scientific temper added to the Constitution
body: The scientific outlook, or scientific temper, is not in the Preamble to the Constitution. It was added to the Fundamental Duties in 1976 through Article 51A(h). Drawing on an essay by historian S. Irfan Habib, Harsh Mander shows that the idea was woven into the freedom struggle and the Constituent Assembly well before that. Nehru was its greatest champion and linked it to freedom from the grip of caste, gender and religion.

For Nehru it was not just a method of the laboratory but a way of living. According to Habib, the scientific temper opposes superstition, not faith. The writer's worry is that reason is retreating from public life today, and that our schooling teaches us to accept tradition without asking questions.

Nor is it a foreign import. The Buddhist, Jain, Samkhya and Charvaka schools questioned dogma. Basava spoke of equality and the dignity of labour, Kabir and Nanak rejected caste, and Akbar built his tolerance on reason. Later came Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj, and Tagore rebuked even Gandhi for calling the 1934 Bihar earthquake divine punishment for untouchability.

Ambedkar saw science as the democratisation of knowledge that the Brahminical order had guarded. In contrast, today Pakistan's textbooks ask children to reject evolution, while Darwin has been removed from India's government textbooks. According to the writer, leaders of the BJP and its allied groups, at times even the Prime Minister, present myths as proof of science, and the director of IIT Madras has called cow urine an important medicine.

The most frightening part is the violence. Dabholkar, Pansare, Kalburgi and Gauri Lankesh paid for reason with their lives, and the writer says full justice for these murders has still not been done. Mander says superstition is now being turned into a weapon and spread in the name of knowledge, and that the fight for the scientific temper is a fight for India's soul.
nazar: The strength of this article is that it presents reason not as something that came from the West but as a home-grown legacy of Kabir, Phule and Ambedkar. To those who call questioning science a defence of 'Indian tradition', that very tradition has an answer: the sharpest questions on this soil were asked of caste, the priest and the scripture.

The poor, Dalits and women carry the heaviest burden of superstition, sometimes as a woman branded a witch and killed, sometimes as a life lost to exorcism. So the removal of Darwin from textbooks is not just a matter of the syllabus. It weakens the citizen who can demand evidence from power.
sawal: How will a child taught without Darwin ever question the Pushpak Vimana?
ref: Article 51A(h)
A Fundamental Duty added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment in 1976. It expects every citizen to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of reform.
Satyashodhak Samaj
Founded by Jotirao Phule in Pune in 1873. Its aim was to spread education and reason against priestly power and caste.
photo_note: A lecture on a model of the planets, Joseph Wright, 1766

h: The big three in Shenzhen: not a new Yalta, just a photo
dek: In Dawn, Mahir Ali writes that the Shenzhen meeting of Xi, Trump and Putin will not shape a new world like Yalta in 1945, and the crisis that most needs talking about is missing from the agenda.
body: In 1945 at Yalta, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin drew the map of the post-war world. Mahir Ali believes the meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen will not turn out like that, and may be no more than a grand photo opportunity. Trump wants to show strength after his embarrassment in the midterm elections, Putin wants to be counted among the 'big three', and Xi is a reluctant host.

The Iran war will be discussed, and according to the writer it is especially painful for China, since it relied on Iranian crude oil. It has cut oil imports and raised exports of green technology such as solar panels. Russia is gaining: sanctions have been eased, and the disruption at Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab has sent its oil exports soaring. Under cover of the US-Israel war, Moscow can also call the Ukraine war a similar security operation.

Nuclear weapons are another knot. In February the Trump administration turned down a Russian offer to extend an arms reduction treaty, because it wants China in any new deal, even though China's arsenal is much smaller than those of the other two. The writer sees America's insistence on keeping China behind in AI by blocking chip exports as probably a lost battle.

The biggest gap is climate, which is not on the agenda at all. It is being discussed at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, where America has no official representative. The writer points to the havoc of a glacier burst in Nepal and an estimated 50,000 deaths from heatwaves in Europe. He also corrects Guterres's remark that the dinosaurs had no lobby: the fossil fuel industry has one, and some of its people may well be sitting in Shenzhen too.
nazar: When three powerful leaders sit down to settle the world's accounts, the Global South is often not at the table but on the menu. Mahir Ali's point speaks directly to India and South Asia: our Himalayan glaciers, our workers in the Gulf and our kitchens hit by costly oil, none of these will be mentioned at a meeting called in the name of 'world peace'.
sawal: Where are Nepal's glaciers on the table in Shenzhen?
ref: Yalta Conference, 1945
A meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin at Yalta in Crimea in the last phase of the Second World War. It settled the post-war division of Europe and the outline of the United Nations.
COP31
The annual UN climate conference, held this year in Antalya, Turkey. It discusses cutting emissions and climate finance for poor countries.
photo_note: The Chess Players, Cornelis de Man

h: Hungry, unpaid and afraid: Africa's journalists
dek: In Al Jazeera, Omar Faruk Osman, president of the Federation of African Journalists, writes that when a journalist is worried about bread and rent, the very foundation of free journalism is hollowed out.
body: Across Africa, journalists are working for months without pay, without contracts and without any protection. According to Omar Faruk Osman, this is an attack on the conditions without which free journalism is impossible. The reporter who is expected to expose corruption is himself trapped in worries about food, rent and bus fare.

With help from UNESCO, the federation carried out the first continent-wide survey of journalists, which drew 1,586 responses from 45 countries. For 61 per cent, earnings do not cover basic needs, 58 per cent are paid late and 62 per cent have no written contract. Even in a relatively strong democracy like Ghana, media workers were earning about 39 to 78 dollars a month.

This affects the news. Investigation, fact-checking and the protection of sources grow weaker, journalists depend on loans, side jobs and 'allowances' from politicians, and the door opens to envelope journalism. 84 per cent censor themselves to some degree, 65 per cent received threats in three years and 78 per cent get no legal help from their employers. Women face the double blow of sexual harassment and lower pay, and 47 per cent have thought of leaving the profession.

But organising has made a difference too. In Mauritania, 1,860 state media workers were made permanent in 2025, in Morocco a union agreement raised pay, and in Namibia a union won a better deal for workers facing layoffs. The writer's demands are: pay on time, written contracts, the right to form unions, worker status for freelancers, investigation of attacks and an end to intimidation through laws. When a journalist has to choose between the truth and survival, it is the public that loses.
nazar: This picture is not Africa's alone. In India's districts and small towns, thousands of stringers work per story, without contracts and without insurance, and they take the greatest risks. The new labour codes also ended the separate status of the Working Journalists Act. Any talk of press freedom is incomplete until it includes the journalist's pay and the union.
sawal: When a reporter's rent is overdue, whose story will he drop?
ref: Envelope journalism
The practice of taking a cash 'allowance' from politicians, companies or officials in return for running or killing a story. In Africa it is called 'brown envelope' journalism.
Federation of African Journalists
A common platform of journalists' unions in African countries, linked to the International Federation of Journalists, that works for journalists' rights and safety.
photo_note: People reading the news, Victor Gilbert

h: From Jamia to Tihar: the price of asking for a students' union
dek: In Navjivan, former Jamia student Zeeshan Ahmad Khan writes that he was sent to Tihar for demanding the return of the students' union, which leaves the question of why the government fears students' unions.
body: In this article Zeeshan Ahmad Khan, a former student of Jamia Millia Islamia who has been linked with the NSUI, tells the story of his time in jail. He reminds us that Jamia is an institution born of the freedom struggle, founded by people like Mohammad Ali Jauhar, Hakim Ajmal Khan and Zakir Husain. To be jailed for asking for a students' union in such an institution seems to him the greatest contradiction.

According to the writer, Jamia's students' union was dissolved in 2006, and there have been no elections for about twenty years since. Citing Aligarh, JNU and Delhi University, he says it is students' unions that prepare tomorrow's leaders.

He gives an account of the agitation in the form of allegations: barricades and police instead of talks, the library shut, classes moved online, and power, water and toilets cut off at the protest site. Paramilitary forces were posted outside the campus along with the Delhi Police. Overnight, slogans that had nothing to do with the demands appeared on the walls, and the students asked for an inquiry.

The writer and his friends were detained outside the campus. They were told they would be let go by evening, but they spent the night at the police station, and the court sent them to Tihar in judicial custody for three days. They refused to sign an apology or a bond. In jail they first met suspicion from other inmates, which he puts down to the image created by the media.

It was in jail that they learned from a newspaper that the registrar had accepted a deadline for drafting a students' union constitution and holding elections, and that their friends on hunger strike for about eighteen days had ended their fast. The writer's conclusion is that as long as students and citizens stand firm, democracy cannot be fully locked up.
nazar: This article is one side's account, and the writer's political ties are plain too, but its core question does not belong to any one party. Twenty years without a students' union election at a central university is in itself a gap in democracy. The promise to meet the demand came only when students were in jail and their friends were starving, which shows how high the price of being heard on campus has become. Now we must see whether the election deadline moves off paper.
sawal: Why did the promise of a students' union come only behind bars?
ref: Jamia Millia Islamia
An institution started in Aligarh in 1920 during the Non-Cooperation Movement, which later moved to Delhi. It became a central university in 1988.
Judicial custody
Keeping an accused person in jail rather than a police station on a court's order. During this time the police need the court's permission to question them.

h: What can a lone referee do on a tilted electoral field
dek: In The News Minute, Srikanth Karwa writes that the debate over the Chief Election Commissioner matters, but the real illness lies in rules that give money and party machinery a free hand.
body: There are petitions against the Chief Election Commissioner in the Supreme Court, and the demand for his resignation has reached the streets. Srikanth Karwa, a student of AI ethics, believes this debate is necessary but incomplete. In his view, even an honest referee cannot level a field whose rules themselves lean one way.

The first question is crime. Citing ADR data, he notes that in 2024, 31 per cent of MPs declared serious criminal cases against themselves, compared with 14 per cent in 2009. The second question is money. In big states a candidate's spending limit is 95 lakh rupees, but the party can spend as much as it likes on the candidate. In 2024 only seven of 3,915 independents won, while 536 party candidates won.

The writer says the 1985 anti-defection law placed the party inside the Constitution, and voters now choose a faction more than a person. Almost 95 per cent of winners from the big parties are crorepatis (millionaires).

His suggestion is state funding. According to International IDEA, 125 of 181 countries give politics public money in some form. He says candidates who win at least five per cent of the vote should be reimbursed up to 75 lakh rupees. Along with this, the spending limit should come down and private donations should be tightened.

He accepts One Nation One Election only if it comes with a constructive no-confidence motion and the repeal of the anti-defection law. He also reminds us that in the 17th Lok Sabha, not even one in ten bills had a recorded vote, so every vote should be public.
nazar: The most useful thing about this article is that it takes anger at the Commission to the question of structure. But we do not agree with the writer's conditional support for One Nation One Election: it remains a danger to the federal structure and to the separate political rhythm of the states. Without curbs on money power and crime, no commissioner, however honest, can open the door for poor and independent candidates.
sawal: Seven of 3,915 independents won. Who did the rest lose to?
ref: ADR
Association for Democratic Reforms, a non-governmental group that works out candidates' assets and criminal cases from their affidavits.
Constructive no-confidence motion
A rule under which a motion to bring down a government must also name the leader of the new government. It has been in force in Germany since 1949.

h: The politics of calling minority welfare 'appeasement'
dek: In Countercurrents, researcher Musharraf Hussain writes that the endlessly repeated word 'appeasement' presents Muslims' constitutional rights as favours and equality as privilege.
body: Musharraf Hussain, an independent researcher in Bengaluru, says the language of politics does not just argue, it also shapes people's identities. Tushtikaran in Hindi, toshon in Bangla and preenanam in Malayalam: these words for 'appeasement' are used again and again on election stages for alleged favouritism towards Muslims. It became a big issue in the recent elections in Bengal and Assam.

The writer agrees that if discrimination in sharing resources is proven, it should be investigated. His objection is to the blind use of this word, which turns every scholarship and every policy to remove backwardness into an unfair favour. He mentions an insulting word used by Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath during the Bengal election campaign in April 2026, which turns a whole community into a cartoon of bigotry.

His argument is that such language erases the line between fair criticism and defaming citizens. On many measures, Muslims are among the most backward communities in the country. Article 14 of the Constitution gives equality, Article 15 protection from discrimination on grounds of religion, and Articles 29 and 30 the cultural and educational rights of minorities. According to the writer, these are not election gifts but constitutional guarantees.

He gives two examples from the world: the image of the 'welfare queen' created in America after the civil rights movement, and the 'swart gevaar', or black danger, of apartheid South Africa. The situations differ, but both show how words breed suspicion against weaker groups.

According to the writer, the danger is that disagreement over policy slowly turns into a question of who belongs to the country. When one community's welfare starts to look like another's loss, an election slogan becomes a social belief.
nazar: The lack of data in the article is a weakness; reports such as the Sachar Committee's could have made the argument more solid. Still, it strikes the right spot. In a country where even a Muslim child's scholarship starts to be viewed with suspicion, the promise of equality stays on paper. Amid news of bulldozers and names struck off in Bengal and Assam, this language is no longer just language.
sawal: How did one child's scholarship come to look like theft from another?
ref: Articles 29 and 30
These articles of the Constitution give minorities the right to protect their language, script and culture and to run their own educational institutions.
Welfare queen
An image in American politics since the 1970s that portrayed Black women who received government help as cheats and lazy.

h: Listen to the farmer before the medicine: the antibiotic crisis in milk
dek: In Down To Earth, dairy sector veteran Kuldeep Sharma writes that the fight against drug resistance will begin by listening to the village livestock keeper, and that the cost of clean milk cannot be put on the small farmer alone.
body: On AMR Awareness Week, Kuldeep Sharma, a long-time expert in the dairy sector, raises a simple question: when an animal falls sick, a doctor and medicine are our answer, but could the illness have been prevented, and does the farmer know what antibiotics do to milk? In his view, the livestock extension service measures success by the number of trainings, not by changes in the farmer's income.

He tells the story of a training in Rajasthan where two hours were spent on azolla fodder. It later turned out that the farmers' animals did not eat azolla at all, that their concern was SNF (solids-not-fat) in milk more than fat, and that for the women the biggest problem was trouble after calving. Had someone simply asked what their biggest difficulty was, the whole session would have changed.

A small farmer's cow kept getting mastitis. The doctor who understood her daily routine caught that one cloth was used on all the teats and that the cow lay down right after milking. A separate towel, cleaning the teats and feeding after milking were enough to fix it.

The real problem is money. After antibiotics, milk cannot be sold for a few days. A farmer who sells 20 litres a day loses the earnings from about 80 litres in four days. Feeding this milk to calves or pigs also raises the risk of drug resistance. One large dairy gave the woman who looks after the animals at home an incentive of one rupee a litre, which brought a family about 600 rupees more a month.

The writer proposes a national mission for contamination-free milk, along the lines of the foot-and-mouth disease and brucellosis campaigns, with prevention, materials in local languages, cheap testing, compensation for losses and a central role for women.
nazar: This article reminds us that drug resistance is a matter not only of the city hospital but also of the village cattle shed. When clean milk protects the health of the whole society, why should its cost come out of the pocket of a family selling twenty litres? Women do most of the work of looking after animals, so no scheme will succeed without listening to them.
sawal: Whose account should four days of thrown-away milk be written into?
ref: AMR
Antimicrobial resistance: when germs such as bacteria get used to medicines and treatment stops working. Careless use of antibiotics in animals is a major cause.
Mastitis
An infection of the udder in dairy animals that reduces and spoils the milk. Dirt and poor milking habits are its main causes.

h: Bengaluru: ragpicker Syed Haji tied up and burnt alive
dek: In a statement before his death, Haji said two strangers lured him to a mound with the promise of plastic, poured petrol on him and set him on fire.
body: Syed Haji, a homeless Muslim who lived by picking scrap in Bengaluru, died on Wednesday evening in the burns ward of Victoria Hospital. Sixty to seventy per cent of his body had been burnt. Before he died, he told the police the whole story in the presence of a doctor.

According to Haji's statement, at a quarter to six on Wednesday morning he was picking scrap on a road in Veerabhadranagar when two strangers came and said there was a lot of plastic and cardboard lying on a mound nearby. There, one of them grabbed him from behind, the two tied his mouth and hands with cloth, poured petrol from a bottle they had brought and set him on fire. They are also accused of taking 600 rupees and his identity card. Haji said he could recognise both of them on sight.

Girinagar police had registered a case of attempted murder against two unknown persons on 18 November, which is now a murder case. The police are looking at CCTV footage. Details of age, home and place differ between the FIR and earlier reports.

So far no relative has come to claim the body, and no post-mortem has been done either, as the department is waiting for a written request from the police. The Karnataka unit of APCR has visited the police station and the mortuary and promised help.
nazar: A man who had no home and no family now has even the investigation into his death stuck waiting on someone. When a basic step like a post-mortem waits on paperwork, justice moves further away from the weakest people. The police must also openly investigate the motive.
sawal: When no one comes to claim the body, who will find the killers?
ref: Dying declaration
A victim's statement recorded before death. Courts treat it as important evidence, since it is believed that a dying man does not lie.
APCR
Association for Protection of Civil Rights. An organisation that gives legal help to victims in civil rights cases.

h: World Court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
dek: The International Court of Justice has for the first time held a country responsible for genocide, but it has no means to enforce its ruling.
body: In The Hague, the highest court of the United Nations, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), held by a majority of 9 judges to 6 that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims and broke the 1948 Genocide Convention. It is the first time the court has directly held a country responsible for genocide. The case was filed by Gambia in 2019.

Court president Yuji Iwasawa said the evidence shows that security forces killed thousands of civilians, carried out sexual violence on a large scale and attacked people as they fled. According to the court, only one reasonable conclusion can be drawn: an intent to destroy a large part of the Rohingya population. In the 2017 crackdown, more than seven and a half lakh Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. Myanmar has maintained that its action was a response to militant attacks.

At the time of that crackdown the army was commanded by Min Aung Hlaing, who is now president. According to Richard Horsey of Crisis Group, it will now be hard for governments that host him to make everything look normal, although the court has no way to enforce its ruling.
Even today about 12 lakh Rohingya live in camps in Bangladesh, where rations have shrunk as aid has fallen.
nazar: This ruling is the first court recognition for people the world ignored for years. India too must now think about how its insistence on calling the Rohingya refugees living here 'infiltrators' and sending them back looks after this ruling.
sawal: Now that genocide is proven, to what land would the Rohingya return?
ref: International Court of Justice (ICJ)
The highest court of the United Nations, which hears disputes between countries. Its ruling is final, with no appeal against it.
Genocide Convention, 1948
An international treaty that makes it a crime to commit violence with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

h: The gram sabha had said no: land acquisition for Dalmia quashed
dek: The Supreme Court said that in a Scheduled Area the prior consent of the gram sabha is essential, and that consent gathered later does not undo the wrong.
body: The Supreme Court has quashed the land acquisition for Dalmia Cement's mining project in three villages of Odisha's Sundargarh district: Kukuda, Bihabandha and Lanjiberna. The bench of Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Satish Chandra Sharma also overturned the Orissa High Court's September 2024 ruling that had upheld the acquisition. The case is Bibol Toppo vs State of Odisha.

Dalmia already held a mining lease until 2040. In 2015 the company sought surface rights over farmland. In January 2020 the gram sabhas (village assemblies) rejected the proposal, yet the state government went ahead.

The court said that since the land was being taken only for a private company's mining, the consent of at least 80 per cent of affected families was needed during the social impact assessment under the 2013 land acquisition law. Because it is a Scheduled Area, the prior consent of the gram sabha was also essential, even if the acquisition was called 'urgent'.

The court found no evidence that the required public hearing on the draft assessment had taken place. Placing one of Dalmia's own consultants in the expert group that reviewed the assessment was also seen as a blow to its independence.
nazar: This ruling is a reminder that a gram sabha's 'no' is not a formality but a legal wall. From Sijimali to Hasdeo, wherever the views of Adivasi (indigenous) villages have been brushed aside, governments should read this ruling carefully.
sawal: If no public hearing was held, how was the acquisition file cleared?
ref: Scheduled Area
Tribal-majority areas declared under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution, where Adivasis have special rights over land and resources.
Social impact assessment
A study required under the 2013 land acquisition law that shows how acquisition will affect people's lives and livelihoods.

h: Citing Dalit students' deaths, plea seeks return of UGC equity rules
dek: Lawyer Anand Jondhale has told the Supreme Court that halting the 2026 rules has left no effective way to complain about discrimination on campus.
body: Lawyer Anand S Jondhale filed an intervention application in the Supreme Court on 17 November, asking that the UGC's 2026 rules to promote equity in higher education institutions be brought back into force. On 29 January the court had stayed these rules and ordered the old 2012 rules to continue.

Jondhale argues that the old framework is incomplete, and that Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe and backward class students pay the price for the lack of an effective complaint system. The objections on which the rules were stayed, such as the definition of caste discrimination and ragging, should be settled by amendment, he says, not by putting the rules in cold storage.

The application lists deaths at IIT Bombay: Aniket Ambhore in 2014, Darshan Solanki in 2023 and Sahil Wakode on 18 September 2026. Sahil's family alleges that he was harassed because of his caste. The institute says he was accused of using a phone in an exam. None of the allegations has yet been proven.

On 5 November the Centre told the court it was thinking of setting up a committee to reconsider the rules. Jondhale wants Dalit, Adivasi and backward class students and teachers to have a place on this committee.
nazar: When such news comes again and again from the same institution over ten years, even an interim stay becomes a decision. If the rules have flaws, they should be fixed, but this gap in between is weighing heaviest on the most vulnerable students.
sawal: Will the committee rethinking the rules include Dalit students?
ref: UGC equity rules 2026
Rules notified on 13 January 2026 that set up committees and a process for complaints of caste discrimination in colleges and universities.
Intervention application
An application made by a third person in an ongoing case, to assist the court or to put forward their own view.

h: Video of Dhaka eviction passed off as Tripura bulldozer action
dek: A BOOM check found that a video said to show Muslim homes being demolished was from Mirpur in Dhaka in May 2026.
body: A video is going round on social media with the claim that Tripura's BJP government is demolishing Muslim homes. It shows women pleading from windows and a structure being torn down. The fact-checking group BOOM has found this claim to be false.

According to BOOM, the video was posted on X on 17 November by an account named Roshni Haokip. The post said that after Bengal and Assam, bulldozer politics had now reached Tripura, and mentioned about 19 thousand families facing eviction in Assam.

A reverse image search of frames from the video led to a 20 May 2026 video from the Bangladeshi channel ATN Bangla News showing the same scene. According to that report, it was part of an eviction drive in Mirpur, Dhaka. The Daily Sun newspaper of the same day wrote that at least seven policemen were injured in protests during the removal of slums from government land in Pallabi, Mirpur.
In other words, the video has nothing to do with Tripura.
nazar: The evictions in Assam are real, but spreading a false video to protest against them weakens that very truth. Those who criticise the government carry a double responsibility, because one wrong clip casts doubt on a hundred true reports.
sawal: How does a fake video weaken protest against real evictions?
ref: Reverse image search
Putting a picture or video frame into a search engine to find out where and when it appeared before.

h: Char Dham Yatra: pilgrims up 29 per cent, deaths from illness up 81 per cent
dek: Figures from Dehradun's SDC Foundation say that before treating record crowds as a success, the mountains' capacity to bear them should be measured.
body: This year 65.6 lakh pilgrims reached Badrinath, Kedarnath, Gangotri, Yamunotri and Hemkund Sahib, about 29 per cent more than last year's 51 lakh. The figures were compiled by Anoop Nautiyal and Praveen Uprety of the SDC Foundation in Dehradun. The reasons given are a longer season, fewer weather disruptions and the shrines staying open for more days.

But deaths rose far faster than the crowds. This season 297 pilgrims died, against 182 last year. Of these, 288 deaths were linked to illness, compared with 159 last year. Kedarnath alone saw 142 deaths. Vehicle traffic also rose by more than 30 per cent, reaching 6.69 lakh by 14 November.

The foundation demands that the carrying capacity of each shrine be assessed: roads, medical care, emergency preparedness, waste, water and the fragile ecology of the Himalaya. It also calls for stronger arrangements for check-ups and treatment along the routes.

At the direction of the National Green Tribunal (NGT), the Wildlife Institute of India has completed this study, but the report is in a sealed envelope. The government says it will make it public only after cabinet approval. The next hearing is on 17 December.
nazar: A government that applauds record crowds is silent on record deaths. Keeping sealed a report that could show the mountains' limits is putting off the safety of both pilgrims and the people who live in the hills.
sawal: Why is the answer to Kedarnath's 142 deaths in a sealed envelope?
ref: Carrying capacity
A scientific estimate of how many people, vehicles and how much construction an area can bear without being damaged.
National Green Tribunal (NGT)
A special court set up in 2010 to hear cases related to the environment.

h: Artists and mayor face off over Thiruvananthapuram's Manaveeyam Veedhi
dek: After cases over a protest meeting and a ban on a singer's programme on the 25-year-old cultural street, artists laid siege to the corporation office, and some were arrested.
body: The 200-metre-long Manaveeyam Veedhi in Thiruvananthapuram has been a home for artists and voices of protest for about 25 years. Now it is at the centre of a clash between the BJP-ruled city corporation and cultural groups.

In October the Collective for Democracy held a meeting here demanding the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, which actor Prakash Raj also attended. Nine organisers were booked for holding a meeting without permission. Then on 14 November, for the street's silver jubilee, a programme was planned by Pushpavathy, a singer known for protest songs, but the corporation refused permission and the police did not allow a microphone to be set up.

Mayor V.V. Rajesh says the action was by the rules and had nothing to do with politics. K.G. Sooraj, convenor of the Manaveeyam Samskarika Koottayma (cultural collective), alleges that the stage for the BJP's march in support of the SIR spread right onto the road, and no one stopped it. Rejecting the mayor's allegation of drugs and sex work, he demanded an apology.

On 16 November cultural groups laid siege to the office of the corporation secretary, the police removed them and some people were arrested. Filmmaker Adoor Gopalakrishnan has written to the culture minister. The minister did not overturn the mayor's decision, and only asked the corporation to reconsider.
nazar: The fight over one street is really about whether the city will keep an open space for dissent. When the procession of those in power gets the road and a song of protest does not get a microphone, it looks less like the rules and more like likes and dislikes.
sawal: Why was the city corporation afraid of Pushpavathy's songs?
ref: Manaveeyam Veedhi
A short road in Thiruvananthapuram chosen in 1999 as an open space for artists, on the lines of Montmartre in Paris. For years plays were staged here every Sunday evening.
ask: Hand over the management of Manaveeyam Veedhi to the Culture Department

h: Rihan dies in Faridabad jail; family alleges torture and extortion
dek: The family of Rihan, 22, who died fifteen days before his wedding, alleges that police gave him electric shocks and extorted Rs 18.8 lakh from them.
body: Rihan Ali, 22, of Jaitoli village in Uttar Pradesh's Amroha district, died in Faridabad jail on 12 November. His family was preparing for his wedding, which was to take place fifteen days later.

The Faridabad Crime Branch had arrested him on 18 October in an alleged robbery of Rs 1.4 crore. The family denies he had any part in it. His uncle Naushad Ali alleges that police also picked up Rihan's elder brother Qasim and father Abdul Sattar, and demanded money by threatening to frame the whole family. According to him, Rs 12.8 lakh was paid first, then six lakh more, for which the family sold four bighas of land.

The family alleges that in custody Rihan was beaten, given electric shocks and burned. Calling from jail, he said he could neither stand nor sit. On the court's orders he was treated at AIIMS. When the body was handed over on 14 November, there were burn marks on his legs and cut wounds in many places. Asked about CCTV, police said the cameras were not working.
There was no statement from the police by the time the story was published. The family wants a fair probe and action against the guilty policemen.
nazar: Every death in custody brings back the same questions: why were the cameras off, where did the wounds come from, and who is accountable. Families like this will not trust the system again unless the probe is handed to an independent agency outside the police.
sawal: Why were the cameras not working while Rihan was in custody?
ref: Custodial death
The death of a person in police or jail custody. By law, every such case needs a magistrate's inquiry and must be reported to the National Human Rights Commission.
ask: A fair probe and punishment for the policemen responsible

h: ASHA workers hold their ground at Freedom Park, turn down CM's appeal
dek: Shivakumar expressed sympathy and asked them to end the sit-in, but ASHA workers said they will not leave until a written order comes.
body: Karnataka's ASHA workers have been on a round-the-clock indefinite sit-in at Bengaluru's Freedom Park since 17 November. Their main demand is an honorarium of Rs 15,000 a month, along with eight or nine other demands.

On Thursday, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar met representatives of the Karnataka State Joint ASHA Workers' Union. He said the government sympathises with them and is not rejecting the honorarium demand, but money is tight and other groups have demands too. According to him, the demands will be discussed with the ministers concerned, in the cabinet and in the coming winter session. He appealed to them to end the sit-in.

The chief minister also laid out the numbers: Rs 2,000 from the Centre, Rs 5,000 from the state and Rs 1,000 as incentive, about Rs 8,000 in all with work-linked allowances. The state has about 41,000 ASHA workers. He asked them to also press the Centre to raise its share.

The workers also complained that they have not been paid dues for work on the special intensive revision (SIR) of voter lists and the educational and social survey. The chief minister promised to release this money. Even so, the workers decided the sit-in will go on until a firm government order comes.
nazar: These women carry the burden of health care in every village, and are also made to do survey and election work, yet their money stays stuck. Statements of sympathy do not fill stomachs, which is why they want the order written on paper.
sawal: Why is the pay for SIR work still held up after the work was done?
ref: ASHA
Accredited Social Health Activist, a role created under the National Rural Health Mission of 2005. They get no salary, only an honorarium and incentives based on the work done.
ask: An honorarium of Rs 15,000 a month and payment of dues

h: Kalamchhuin villagers halt two coal mines in Talcher
dek: A protest since 16 November has stopped work at the Hingula and Balram mines, and the dispute is stuck on where the resettlement colony should be.
body: A protest by the people of Kalamchhuin village in Odisha's Talcher coalfield has stopped work at Mahanadi Coalfields Limited's (MCL) Hingula and Balram opencast mines since 16 November. This information is based on the company's own statement.

According to MCL, the production and dispatch of about 60,000 tonnes of coal a day has stopped, and transport to the siding has also halted. The company calls this a loss to itself and to the state treasury.

One of the villagers' demands has already been met: the district administration has given a written assurance that the shifting of Hingula High School to Gobindpasi will be stopped. But the real fight is over the resettlement site. The villagers want to be settled in Ekatalsahi. MCL says that area sits on coal-bearing land, so a colony cannot be built there, and it has offered Jamunali and Kochhianali as options.

The company has offered about 950 jobs for displaced families and Rs 25 lakh in cash in place of a plot, and says about 200 families have already chosen cash. Still, the villagers have not let mining restart. The report does not carry the villagers' own side.
nazar: When a mine stops, the loss is counted in tonnes and rupees, but the loss of a village being uprooted is never entered in any ledger. If people want to settle at a place of their choice, that is not stubbornness. It is a question of their voice in resettlement.
sawal: Why are the people of Kalamchhuin set on Ekatalsahi alone?
ref: Talcher coalfield
A large coal area in Odisha's Angul district, where MCL runs several opencast mines. As the mines have spread, the displacement and resettlement of villages here has been a constant dispute.
ask: Build the resettlement colony at Ekatalsahi

h: AAMSU takes fight against selective evictions to Delhi, appeals to President
dek: After a four-day programme, the All Assam Minority Students' Union submitted a ten-point memorandum to the President.
body: The All Assam Minority Students' Union (AAMSU) held a four-day programme in Delhi from 14 to 17 November against what it calls the selective eviction of Muslims in Assam. It included a protest at Ramlila Maidan, a seminar at V.K. Menon Bhawan near the Supreme Court, a press conference and memorandums to officials.

AAMSU president Imtiaz Hussain alleges that non-Muslims in the same areas are not being removed, and that about a hundred mosques, madrasas and dargahs have been demolished, but not a single temple. He said that if encroachments are to be removed, the law must apply equally to all. He also accused Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma of creating a communal atmosphere.

The ten-point memorandum sent to the President demands that arbitrary evictions stop at once, that uprooted families be resettled, and that there be a clear policy for giving land leases (pattas) to the landless. It also seeks a review of the Foreigners Tribunal Order 1964, a probe into delimitation, no special summary revision for now, identity cards for everyone included in the final NRC, and fair action against those spreading hate.
The report carries no response from the Assam government or the Election Commission.
nazar: The question of evictions has now moved out of Assam and reached the capital. If removing encroachments is truly a matter of law, the government has to show that the bulldozer does not look at religion before it moves, and say where those whose homes were razed will find a roof.
sawal: In the same village, whose home was spared and whose was razed?
ref: Foreigners Tribunal
Quasi-judicial bodies in Assam that decide whether a person is a foreigner or not. Their process and rulings have long been questioned.
place: Ramlila Maidan, Delhi (for evicted families of Assam)
ask: Stop selective evictions and resettle uprooted families

h: Yamunanagar sugarcane farmers to sit in at agriculture minister's home
dek: The Bharatiya Kisan Union has decided on an indefinite round-the-clock sit-in outside minister Shyam Singh Rana's home in Radaur, calling a rise of 15 paise a kilo a joke.
body: In Haryana's Yamunanagar district, the Bharatiya Kisan Union has decided to hold an indefinite sit-in from 21 November at agriculture minister Shyam Singh Rana's home in Radaur, to push for a higher sugarcane price. The decision was taken at a meeting of the union's 11-member committee at the PWD rest house in Jagadhri.

District president Subhash Gurjar said the sit-in will run day and night, and farmers will be given duties block by block. At ten in the morning on 21 November, farmers will gather at the Radaur market committee office, march to the minister's home raising slogans, and pitch tents there. The sit-in will not end until the government raises the price.

Gurjar says the government is not taking farmers' demands seriously. He called the recent rise of 15 paise a kilo in the cane price a joke on farmers, and said there has been no decent rise in the price for 12 years.

According to him, the Samyukt Kisan Morcha, led by leaders such as Ratan Maan and Suresh Kauth, is protesting at sugar mills across the state. The next big step will come on 2 December, when farmers from across the state will surround the chief minister's residence in Kurukshetra.
nazar: A cane farmer's costs rise every year with fertiliser, diesel and labour, but the price moves by paise. The decision to pitch tents at the minister's door shows that the voices outside the mills are not reaching Chandigarh.
sawal: What will a rise of 15 paise a kilo change for a farmer?
ref: State advised price for sugarcane
Some states set their own higher price above the Centre's minimum price (FRP), called the SAP. In Haryana, sugar mills buy cane from farmers at this price.
ask: A decent rise in the sugarcane price

h: To save their fields, farmers fought an election, and two won
dek: Against the taking of 855 acres of fertile land for a Reliance AI data centre in Bhogapuram, Andhra Pradesh, farmers turned the mandal election itself into their battleground.
body: In Bhogapuram, a coastal village in Vizianagaram district about forty kilometres from Visakhapatnam, a group of farmers contested three mandal parishad seats on a single issue: no data centre. Independent candidates Alla Saroja and Godla Seshagiri won, and Kolli Srinu lost. According to the report, this is the first election in the country fought on this question.

The fight is over a one-gigawatt AI data centre of Reliance Industries, said to cost about Rs 1.08 lakh crore. A government order of May 2026 set aside 854.97 acres of farmland in Bhogapuram and Polipalli for it. The company will get a 25 per cent discount on the land price and years of concessions on power, water and taxes. These fields give two or three crops a year, and the government buys the paddy grown here for the ration system.

The High Court said private land can be taken only with consent or according to the law, yet a notification for about 830 acres was issued in September. The report says a 2018 order exempted this project from key parts of the 2013 land acquisition law, meaning no social impact assessment and no public hearing. When parties did not back them even after a sit-in of two hundred and fifty days, the farmers entered the field themselves.

In Polipalli the protest is muted. There, about 38 acres of assigned land belonging to some 40 Dalit families falls within the plan, land that by law cannot be sold. These daily wage families are afraid to speak openly.

Alla Saroja, a homemaker, is now the best known voice of the group. Officials say objections will be heard and compensation has not yet been fixed. The farmers are preparing to go back to the High Court.
nazar: The data centre is being sold as 'the future', but its price is being paid by villages that were never even asked. If land is taken by exempting it from the very law that made consent and social assessment necessary, that is not development; it is pushing democracy aside. The farmers of Bhogapuram have shown that when parties stay silent, the ballot box too can become a tool of resistance.
sawal: Why servers in place of fields that grow paddy for rations?
ref: RFCTLARR Act, 2013

The law on fair compensation and transparency in land acquisition.
For private projects it makes the consent of 80 per cent of affected families and a social impact assessment necessary.
Assigned land

Land given by the government to landless, often Dalit, families.
Under Andhra's 1977 law it cannot be sold or transferred.

h: Kachchh's herder women: the milk is theirs, the earnings someone else's
dek: Among the Maldhari communities of Kachchh, as the nomadic life faded, women's work grew, but their say over money, decisions and movement shrank.
body: In Mori, a coastal village of Lakhpat bordering Pakistan, Achhat Bai Jat, 57, waits for her buffaloes in the evening. She is a Fakirani Jat, from a nomadic camel herding community. She began grazing with her mother at the age of five, when the family had nearly a hundred camels; today she looks after more than a hundred and fifty buffaloes. From four in the morning, fodder, cleaning and milking are the women's job.

According to Marhaba Hilali's report, Achhat Bai's milk goes to Sarhad Dairy, but the payment message comes on her brother's phone, because the dairy has his name on record. A hundred litres of milk brings about five thousand rupees, but in this year of drought two thousand of that goes on water for the animals.

Of 75-year-old Nasibi Ben's two hundred Kharai camels, only fifty are left. According to the organisation Sahjeevan, the number of Kharai camels has fallen from ten thousand to about one thousand in two decades. Border restrictions, forest department bans, ports and solar projects kept swallowing the grazing land. The earnings of Gulnaz Mutva of Gorewali village in Banni also go into her husband's account.

The elderly Rabari women of Bhadroi village remember that they too once walked hundreds of kilometres with the herds. Kriti Laheru of the Kutch Mahila Vikas Sangathan says settling down increased women's burden and reduced their voice in household decisions. In herders' organisations, women are members in name only.
Many women have no birth certificate, no Aadhaar and no ration card, so government schemes do not reach them. In Mori, tap water comes once in ten days. Still, Achhat Bai wants to remain a herder.
nazar: Behind the shine of the White Revolution are women whose hands draw the milk but whose names are not on the account. If a cooperative dairy is truly a cooperative, the payment should be in the name of the woman who does the work. Before forcing solar and industrial projects onto grazing land, the families whose generations grew up on this land must be asked.
sawal: Why does the dairy not pay the woman who milks the animals?
ref: Maldhari

Livestock herding communities of Kachchh and Saurashtra, including Muslim Jats and Mutvas and Hindu Rabaris.
Traditionally nomadic, now mostly semi-nomadic or settled.
Kharai camel

A camel breed of Kachchh that swims out to graze in the sea mangroves.
Bans on mangrove access and grazing have made its numbers fall fast.

h: Rahi Masoom Raza: I am Hindustani, I will write the Mahabharat
dek: A 49-minute conversation with Rahi Masoom Raza's daughter Maryam: an 850 square foot rented home, 'Aadha Gaon' written in Urdu, and the case of the 'Hindustani' who wrote the 'Mahabharat'.
by: Maryam Moonis Raza, with Parvez Alam
body: This conversation takes place on the occasion of Rahi Masoom Raza's birth centenary, but it is no polished poster of his life. In Cine Ink's podcast 'London Varta' (London Talks), Parvez Alam speaks with his daughter Maryam Moonis Raza, who lives in America. She says that for the world this is a centenary year; for her it is one more year spent without her father.

Raza was born on 1 August 1927 in Gangoli, a village in Ghazipur, the same village that returns in 'Aadha Gaon' (Half a Village). Tuberculosis of the bone sent him to the sanatorium at Bhowali, then came a PhD in Aligarh on 'Tilism-e-Hoshruba' and the art of dastangoi (storytelling), and a lecturer's post. There he fell in love with Nayyar Jahan, who was already married and the mother of three sons. The marriage became a scandal, he was accused of 'moral turpitude', he did not get the temporary lectureship, and in 1966 the family settled in Bombay.

The Bombay home was a rented flat of 850 square feet: Ammi and Papa, four children, two parrots, a dog, staff and guests all day. Qawwali by the Sabri Brothers in the sitting room, Led Zeppelin from the son's room, and four or five guests at dinner. On Papa's birthday, food for 50 or 60 people was cooked in that same house, and he wrote amid that same noise.

There was no writing desk: he would lie on the floor against a bolster, writing by hand in both Hindi and Urdu, and later on a Hindi-English typewriter. Once Raaj Kumar took him to Kashmir and he could not write a single word there; he used to say he could not write unless the voices of his family were in his ears. People came and went until one or two at night, then he wrote novels and poetry, and at half past seven in the morning he was at breakfast with the children.

In films he wrote dialogue and screenplays for up to 150 or 200 films: 'Mili', 'Golmaal', 'Alaap', 'Disco Dancer', 'Karz', 'Lamhe'; some songs too. Raj Khosla, Hrishikesh Mukherjee, B.R. Chopra and Majrooh Sultanpuri came to the house. He first turned down the offer of the 'Mahabharat'; Chopra announced that he would write it anyway, and then letters came like this: was there only one Muslim to be found for the Mahabharat? Reading the letters, he said, now I will certainly write it, I am Hindustani, I grew up in Ghazipur. Bigots on both sides sent threats; he did not budge. He spoke out fearlessly against the Emergency too; that night there was fear of arrest.

'Aadha Gaon' was originally written in Urdu. The Anjuman Taraqqi-e-Urdu Hind refused to publish it; in 1966 it came out in Hindi and reached every home; several editions followed, and later it came from Rajkamal. Maryam says many Urdu idioms and terms from the marsiya (elegy) were cut from the Hindi edition. The handwritten Urdu manuscript survived among Ammi's papers at Aftab Manzil, and now Athar Farouqui of the Anjuman is publishing it in the centenary year. Raza died in Bombay in 1992 and is buried there; Nayyar Jahan died in America in 2021. The conversation ends on lines from 'Ajnabi Shehar' (Strange City), sung by Jagjit Singh.
nazar: This conversation is not just a daughter's memories. It also holds an era when a writer had to pay for calling himself 'Hindustani' with the bigotry of both sides, and he paid it. The return of the Urdu manuscript of 'Aadha Gaon' reopens a debate we too easily reduce to a quarrel over language: the language a book was written in and the language it was published in have never been the same thing.
sawal: Why was a book written in Urdu not published in Urdu?
ref: London Varta
Cine Ink's Hindi-Urdu podcast, in which Parvez Alam holds long conversations with writers and artists.
Aadha Gaon
Rahi Masoom Raza's best known novel, the story of a Ghazipur village before and after Independence.
Anjuman Taraqqi-e-Urdu Hind
An old institution for the Urdu language and literature, which in the 1960s refused to publish the Urdu manuscript of 'Aadha Gaon'.

h: 'B Three' on an open lawn: the Blackboard Brigade and Osavari, who asks questions
dek: Aditya Pandey watches Shahid Anwar's play 'B Three' take shape from rehearsal to stage, and says the play hands its audience not applause but a question.
body: Watching a play is one thing, and watching it being made is quite another. Aditya Pandey got this chance at the invitation of a friend, who asked him to watch a rehearsal and give his opinion. The rush behind the stage, actors forgetting their lines and slowly growing into their characters: he saw all this up close for the first time.

The play was 'B Three', written by Shahid Anwar and presented by University Theatre and Swaraj Vidyapeeth. It was directed by Amitesh Kumar, a teacher in the Hindi department. According to the writer, he asked the actors for their views after every rehearsal. It was staged on the evening of 4 November on the open lawn of the Vidyapeeth, while during rehearsals roof-casting machines nearby kept competing with the actors' voices.

The play moves in several layers. One layer shows the cost of leaning entirely on one man or one power. In another, education under the pressure of profit turns students into machines instead of thinking human beings. One scene, through talks between representatives of different countries, satirises the hypocrisy of markets and diplomacy. The 'B Three' of the title is really the 'Blackboard Brigade', which imposes blind nationalism with the help of a slogan that calls pride itself a virtue.

At the centre is Osavari, who asks questions and refuses to accept the pride forced on her. A character named Satsangi grows violent with the backing of the organisation and pushes her towards death. The writer sees this character as a symbol of that part of ordinary people who have no separate identity of their own left.

The writer found the first rehearsal a little dull, but on the final evening the lights, music and acting changed his mind. According to him, after the show the audience carried home Osavari's own question: what was her fault?
nazar: Campus theatre today is one of the few places where fascism can be discussed openly, and that too amid noisy machines, without a big budget. In Deshkaal's view it matters that such plays are documented, because characters like Osavari are not far from real faces in universities today.
sawal: How long does a slogan written on the blackboard last in a classroom?
ref: Shahid Anwar
A Hindi playwright whose plays sharply satirise contemporary politics and society.
Swaraj Vidyapeeth
An educational and cultural platform linked to Swaraj Bhawan, where 'B Three' was staged on the open lawn.

h: An old notebook, pencil marks and the road to poetry
dek: In the second part of his series, Shachindra Arya looks back at the early poems that came out of newspapers, television and novels and were set down in a notebook.
body: Shachindra Arya admits he never really thought about how a poem is actually written. Last month, while cleaning up, he came across an old notebook in which his early poems were written down with rough titles. They carried pencil marks, as if he had been testing whether a poem survives when a word or a line is removed.

That notebook has a poem about a boy and a girl who never met alone under the open sky, and who say nothing in the poem either. One poem was a satire on TV coverage of an American president's visit to India. The writer copied it by hand, saved a photocopy, and showed it in a corridor to Sanjeev Kumar, a critic at Deshbandhu College. He no longer remembers the response, and both copies of the poem are lost too.

Some poems came from the street, like a thin mother begging at a red light, a scene the writer says was really from the Faiz Road signal. Some came from reading, like a poem of the same name after reading Kamleshwar's 'Kitne Pakistan' (How Many Pakistans), which was printed in the college's annual magazine 'Desh'. One poem came from a character in a Doordarshan telefilm, a man at a ration office who gives every visitor a long lecture on culture and history.

The writer remembers a cold evening when, after reading Sudhish Pachauri's short piece on 'Sholay' in 'Rashtriya Sahara', he wrote a diary entry in the same style while watching the film on TV. He asks whether this was imitation or something else, and believes the wish to write poetry woke from this experience.
He has always found it hard to bring the plain, clear speech of the diary into poetry. The essay ends with 'to be continued': for the writer, the question is still more interesting than any answer.
nazar: In Hindi, stories of becoming a poet often begin with a guru or some big event. Shachindra's story feels truer: a newspaper column, a TV film, a woman standing at a red light. In Deshkaal's view it is a reminder that the raw material of the new generation's poetry is still the everyday city and its media.
sawal: What does a line struck out in pencil take away from a poem?
ref: Kitne Pakistan
Kamleshwar's novel published in 2000, written in the form of a court hearing on Partition and the violence of history.
Sudhish Pachauri
A Hindi critic and columnist who has long written on media and popular culture.
photo_note: Rabindranath in the role of the blind singer, 1916

h: A poem reaches us as a picture before it reaches us as meaning
dek: Young poet Vidhan Gunjan's critical essay traces the role of image and symbol from Bhimbetka through the Bhakti age to Muktibodh.
body: Vidhan Gunjan's argument is simple: a poem does not become a poem through meaning and clever words alone. While writing, an image first rises in the poet's mind, and the whole frame of the poem is built on it. As rhythm is to music, image and symbol are to poetry.

According to the writer, symbols and images are a way of expressing an abstract feeling through a concrete thing, person, event or place. Darkness becomes a symbol of despair, ignorance and fear; light, of hope and moving forward. Because symbols are rooted in culture, they cross borders and reach the reader.

The essay makes an interesting comparison. The Indus Valley script has not been read to this day, but scholars have been able to understand the paintings in the Bhimbetka caves. From this the writer concludes that humans understood signs before letters, and that language grew out of that world of signs.

Then he turns to the tradition of Hindi poetry. Tulsi and Sur built Ram and Sita and Krishna's play out of images; Kabir used the symbols of musk and the deer to say that what you seek outside is within. In Chhayavad, Prasad, Nirala, Pant and Mahadevi made nature the vehicle of human feeling. Later, Muktibodh, Dhoomil and Sarveshwar made symbols a tool of change and revolt.

In the end the writer returns to Acharya Ramchandra Shukla's point that in poetry we take in pictures more than meaning. His advice is that readers should go beyond dictionary meanings and also hear the pictures words make, and their sound.
nazar: This essay is less a new thesis than a young poet's reflection on his own craft, and that is its strength. In Deshkaal's view the mention of Muktibodh and Dhoomil matters: a symbol is not just decoration; it has also been a language for confronting power directly, especially when saying things plainly becomes costly.
sawal: We could read Bhimbetka's paintings, so why not the Indus script?
ref: Bhimbetka
Prehistoric caves in Madhya Pradesh whose rock paintings are thousands of years old and are listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Chhayavad
A Hindi poetry movement of the early decades of the twentieth century, in which nature, love and personal feeling were central.
photo_note: Radha and Krishna watching a storm, Kangra style

h: Boys swinging the ball, not running away but running on
dek: Javed Alam Khan's long poem tells the story of small-town boys who, dreaming of fast bowling, want to get past poverty, family duties and fear.
body: Sammukh has published a long poem by Javed Alam Khan whose title is its key: they are not running away, they are running. The poem is about boys who practise fast bowling on some ground. They stand at the meeting point of two centuries and two stages of life, between boyhood and youth, and the dream of making the ball swing outweighs the hardship around them.

The motion of swinging the arm returns again and again in the poem, slowly becoming a refrain: restlessness, irritation and hope, all three in that one swing. Along with the seam of the ball, the pitch, the stumps and the crease come heroes like Waqar Younis, Kapil Dev, Sachin and Lara.

The inner world of these boys is made of films, novels and comics. Their sentimentality over the characters of 'Devdas' and 'Chitralekha' and the influence of comic heroes like Nagraj, Doga and Dhruv mix into their game. They keep the fast in Ramzan, offer namaz on time, and also swear and rebel. The poem lets faith and defiance live together in one body.

Between games there are chores at home too: trips to the market and the flour mill, jobs, love and the fear of tomorrow. In the end the race leaves the ground and becomes the race of life. The boys have left behind the ground, the town, the state and their youth, yet they are still running, and the poem asks what this longing should be called.

Javed Alam Khan's collections 'Syah Waqt ki Ibaraten' (Writings of a Dark Time, 2023) and 'Saleeb par Nagrikta' (Citizenship on the Cross, 2026) have been published. The full poem can be read on Sammukh.
nazar: This poem sees small-town Muslim boys the way any boy should be seen: full of dreams, irritation, cricket and books. In Deshkaal's view, in today's climate, when such boys are often shown only through the lens of suspicion, this difference between 'running away' and 'running' is also a political statement.
sawal: How far will the boy copying Waqar Younis get?
ref: Reverse swing
The skill of fast bowlers with an old ball in which the ball swings the opposite way; Waqar Younis is regarded as a master of it.
Saleeb par Nagrikta
Javed Alam Khan's poetry collection published in 2026.

h: Patients crossing rivers, and the Aadhaar queue
dek: Renu Khanna's review says Dr Ramani Atkuri's book 'Staying Alive' draws on four decades of experience to record the failures of India's public health system.
body: Dr Ramani Atkuri has worked in public health in central India for nearly four decades. Since the 1990s she has been a doctor, trainer and researcher in remote areas of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Rajasthan. Her book 'Staying Alive', published by Pan Macmillan, is a mix of memoir and critique.

According to reviewer Renu Khanna, the book's central question is why avoidable deaths happen in remote areas while the urban rich and medical tourists get the best care. In one chapter a man working in a field at night was probably bitten by a krait; he survived because he reached a medical college in time and got a ventilator. Primary health centres often do not even have anti-snake venom.

Other chapters are on displacement. When Chhattisgarh's Achanakmar forest was made a tiger reserve, the Adivasis (indigenous people) who were moved out saw their food, income and social fabric fall apart, and drinking rose among the men. One chapter shows how, with no roads, bridges or vehicles, precious time for treatment is lost crossing rivers. There is also a separate chapter on access to legal abortion for single women and minor girls.

The book says compulsory digitisation linked to Aadhaar shuts the most vulnerable people out of care, and records frontline workers' complaint that tablets have taken their time away from care and put it into filling registers. According to the review, government spending on health is 1.84 per cent of GDP, while the National Health Policy of 2017 had promised 2.5 per cent.

The book does not only complain. The chapter 'Jholawale' (the activists with cloth bags) sets out experiments by organisations that could be scaled up. Khanna calls it an essential book for policymakers and students of health.
nazar: Atkuri's book reminds us that the health crisis begins well before the hospital wall: on a broken bridge, in a village that was uprooted, in a queue where Aadhaar does not work. In Deshkaal's view, when health's share of the budget lags behind the government's own promise, such testimony gives a truer picture than official figures.
sawal: How far is a ventilator from a patient bitten by a krait?
ref: Achanakmar Tiger Reserve
A tiger sanctuary in the Bilaspur-Mungeli area of Chhattisgarh, from which several Adivasi villages were moved out.
National Health Policy 2017
A central government policy that set the goal of raising government spending on health to 2.5 per cent of GDP by 2025.
photo_note: South Indian villagers going to market, 1937

h: Cooch Behar: ten kilos of salt and a boy's life
dek: Former IAS officer Chandan Sinha's memoir essay shows how Partition and barbed wire turned centuries-old trade into 'smuggling'.
body: In June 2001 Chandan Sinha arrived in Cooch Behar as district magistrate. Within a month a wireless message came from Dinhata police station: the BSF had fired on smugglers crossing the barbed wire on the Bangladesh border. A boy of thirteen or fourteen was killed, and a sack of ten kilos of salt was found at the spot. The writer admits he had no idea salt could be so precious.

Over three years many such messages came, each time about salt or some everyday item. To understand this, the writer turns to history. The district begins in the Terai and spreads across plains made by rivers, where about thirty rivers flow from north-west to south-east, change course and leave behind beels.

Before 1947, rice went from here to the Dooars and the tea gardens of Assam, while jute, tobacco and mustard went to Calcutta and Dhaka. The rivers were the trade routes. River landings called 'bandar', such as Gitaldaha, Tufanganj and Natabari, handled the goods, and across the border Mogalhat and Lalmonirhat in Rangpur were big centres.

Partition cut this bond. The nearby buyers of jute and tobacco were lost, the rivers kept flowing but trade no longer flowed with them, and the landings decayed into weekly haats (markets). Even so, for years people from both sides kept coming and going to these haats. Fencing began in 1986, and according to the writer it was still unfinished in 2001 and is still going on today.

Where the wire went up, the trader from across could no longer set up shop and the customer could no longer come over. Dealings that had been lawful for centuries became a crime overnight. The writer argues that this 'smuggling' of bicycles, cloth, spices, sugar and salt is the child of a broken regional economy, whose price that boy paid with his life.
nazar: The strength of this essay is that it begins with a government officer's confession: he did not know. In Deshkaal's view it is easy to call the poor of border districts 'smugglers' and 'infiltrators'; this essay shows that the line drawn on the map first took away their livelihood and then branded them criminals.
sawal: When the river landings decayed, where did the traders of the haats go?
ref: Bangnama

Crescent-shaped lakes formed when rivers change course, common in the plains of north Bengal and Assam.
